objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with chronic left shoulder pain without a history of trauma.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Over the past two months, I’ve had insidious left shoulder pain that’s been getting worse, especially at the extreme ranges of motion and when I’m active. It’s started to disrupt my sleep and makes daily tasks like brushing my hair and dressing difficult.
What is your age, and have you had any recent trauma or injury to the shoulder, even minor?
I’m 55 years old, and I haven’t had any shoulder trauma or injury—nothing even minor.
When you completely relax your arm and someone else tries to move it, is the motion restricted by stiffness, or does the full movement cause pain but the range itself is preserved?

“It feels more like pain at the extremes when someone moves it, rather than a hard stiffness where the motion is blocked—though it definitely becomes very painful when I reach the limit. The movement range seems mostly preserved, but the end range triggers the worst pain.”
Where exactly is the pain located—is it on the top/outside of the shoulder (over the deltoid), the front of the shoulder, or deep within the joint?
“It’s mainly deep within the joint and feels more toward the front/upper part of the shoulder rather than right on the outside over the deltoid.”
When you try to lift your arm out to the side or rotate it outward against resistance, does it feel weak, or is it primarily just painful but with normal strength?
“It’s primarily painful, not weak—I can still lift and rotate it, but it hurts a lot when I move it outward or try to rotate it against resistance.”
Do you feel any grinding, clicking, or catching sensations when you move your shoulder?
I don’t notice much grinding or clicking, and I haven’t felt any catching sensations—mostly it’s just sharp pain when I get to the extreme positions.
Do you have any neck pain, or does the pain radiate down your arm toward your hand?
“No neck pain, and it doesn’t radiate down my arm toward my hand—I keep feeling it mainly in the left shoulder itself. I also haven’t had any numbness or tingling or weakness in my arm or hand.”
When you lift your arm out to the side, is the pain worst in the middle of the movement (between shoulder height and straight up), or only when you reach the very top?
"It’s worst when I reach the very top of the motion—near the extreme positions. Between shoulder height and straight up it’s still painful, but it really spikes at the end range."
When you lie on your left side in bed, does that specifically trigger or worsen the shoulder pain?
“Yes, lying on my left side definitely worsens the pain and makes it harder to stay comfortable, and it can disrupt my sleep.”
Do you have diabetes, thyroid disease, or have you had any recent prolonged immobilization of the shoulder (such as after surgery or injury to another arm/shoulder)?
“Yes, I have type 2 diabetes, and I take metformin and glipizide. I don’t have any known thyroid disease, and I haven’t had any recent surgery or immobilization of the shoulder.”

If you stand with your left elbow bent at 90 degrees against your side and relax, can someone else rotate your forearm outward (away from your body) as far as on your right side, or does it stop short even when you try to relax?

“Yes—on my left side, when someone tries to rotate my forearm outward, it doesn’t feel blocked by a hard stop, but I can’t comfortably go as far; it becomes sharply painful at the end range, whereas the right side allows full motion without that spike.”
Do you have any pain, stiffness, or similar symptoms in your right shoulder or any other joints?

“I don’t really have similar pain or problems in my right shoulder, and I haven’t noticed these kinds of symptoms in my other joints—this has been mainly the left shoulder. Occasionally I’ll feel general aches from time to time, but not the same pattern of deep, end-range pain. How would you like me to describe it next?”
When you try to reach behind your back with your left hand (for example, to tuck in your shirt or reach your back pocket), how high up can you get your thumb compared to your right side
“It hurts and limits me when I try to reach behind my back, and my left thumb can’t get as high as on the right—I can feel the sharp end-range pain before I reach the same level.”
[DDX] Adhesive capsulitis (primary frozen shoulder), Rotator cuff tendinopathy with secondary impingement, Glenohumeral osteoarthritis, Calcific tendinitis, Bicipital tendinopathy
